claim: In the MMTV-PyMT transgenic mammary cancer model on FVB mice, voluntary running had no statistically significant effect on tumor growth.
source: Contrary to what was previously shown (Goh et al., 2013), the running mice in our experiments showed no statistically significant differences in tumor growth between the groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C- G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no statistically significant differences in tumor growth were observed between running and non-running groups in the MMTV-PyMT model, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-G.

claim: Voluntary running increased infiltration of Granzyme B (GZMB)-positive cells in primary tumors of MMTV-PyMT mice.
source: However, the infiltration of Granzyme B (GZMB)-positive cells was significantly higher in primary tumors of running mice, even though voluntary running had no effect on the frequency of CD3, F4/80, PCNA, or podocalyxin-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript states that GZMB-positive cell infiltration was significantly higher in running mice, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Voluntary running had no effect on the frequency of CD3, F4/80, PCNA, or podocalyxin-expressing cells in primary tumors of MMTV-PyMT mice.
source: However, the infiltration of Granzyme B (GZMB)-positive cells was significantly higher in primary tumors of running mice, even though voluntary running had no effect on the frequency of CD3, F4/80, PCNA, or podocalyxin-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that voluntary running had no effect on these cell populations, with data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Exercise modulates the infiltration of cytotoxic lymphocytes in the MMTV-PyMT tumor model.
source: This indicates that exercise in this tumor model modulates the infiltration of cytotoxic lymphocytes.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation of the data showing increased GZMB-positive cells in tumors from running mice.

claim: Infiltration of cytotoxic T cells is linked to a favorable prognosis in many human neoplasms and in some animal tumor models.
source: Given that infiltration of cytotoxic T cells is linked to a favorable prognosis in many human neoplasms and in some animal tumor models (Savas et al., 2016), we proceeded to explore the role of lymphoid cells, and in particular cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, on the process of exercise-induced reduction of tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Savas et al., 2016.

claim: The progression of the transgenic MMTV-PyMT model is predominantly regulated by myeloid cells.
source: As the progression of the transgenic MMTV-PyMT model is predominantly regulated by myeloid cells (Lin et al., 2003), we carried out a further set of experiments, wherein immunocompetent FVB mice were given access to an exercise wheel 14 days prior to, and then following, subcutaneous injection with a murine mammary cancer line derived from the MMTV-PyMT model, the I3TC cell line (Weiland et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2003.

claim: In the I3TC subcutaneous tumor model, allowing FVB animals to exercise significantly reduced tumor growth.
source: In this cell-line-driven model, allowing animals to exercise significantly reduced tumor growth and increased survival times (Figure 1B) relative to animals not given access to an exercise wheel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise reduced tumor growth, with data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the I3TC subcutaneous tumor model, allowing FVB animals to exercise increased survival times.
source: In this cell-line-driven model, allowing animals to exercise significantly reduced tumor growth and increased survival times (Figure 1B) relative to animals not given access to an exercise wheel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise increased survival times, with data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the I3TC subcutaneous tumor model, only CD8+ T cells showed a significant increase in frequency across tumor, spleen, and lymph nodes in running animals.
source: Here, only CD8+ T cells showed a significant increase in frequency across these three tissues in the running animals (Figure 1E); no significant changes were seen in the frequency of CD4+ T cells, NK cells (Figure 1C and D), or intra-tumoral macrophages or neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that only CD8+ T cells showed significant increases, with data shown in multiple figures.

claim: In the I3TC subcutaneous tumor model, no significant changes were seen in the frequency of CD4+ T cells, NK cells, intra-tumoral macrophages, or neutrophils in running animals.
source: Here, only CD8+ T cells showed a significant increase in frequency across these three tissues in the running animals (Figure 1E); no significant changes were seen in the frequency of CD4+ T cells, NK cells (Figure 1C and D), or intra-tumoral macrophages or neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no significant changes were observed in these cell populations, with data shown in multiple figures.

claim: CD8+ T-cell depletion via weekly injections of anti-CD8 antibodies reduced the CD8+ population in both spleen and tumor.
source: The CD8+ T-cell depletion reduced the CD8+ population of both the spleen (Figure 1F) and the tumor (Figure 1G), and significantly reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on both tumor growth (Figure 1H) and long-term survival (Figure 1I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that CD8+ depletion reduced CD8+ populations, with data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: CD8+ T-cell depletion significantly reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on tumor growth in the I3TC model.
source: The CD8+ T-cell depletion reduced the CD8+ population of both the spleen (Figure 1F) and the tumor (Figure 1G), and significantly reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on both tumor growth (Figure 1H) and long-term survival (Figure 1I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that CD8+ depletion reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on tumor growth, with data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: CD8+ T-cell depletion significantly reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on long-term survival in the I3TC model.
source: The CD8+ T-cell depletion reduced the CD8+ population of both the spleen (Figure 1F) and the tumor (Figure 1G), and significantly reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on both tumor growth (Figure 1H) and long-term survival (Figure 1I).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that CD8+ depletion reduced the beneficial effects of exercise on survival, with data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Cytotoxic T-cells play a clear role in the suppression of tumor growth by exercise in the I3TC model.
source: This depletion study demonstrates a clear role for cytotoxic T-cells in the suppression of tumor growth by exercise in this model.
evidence: This is an explicit conclusion drawn from the CD8+ depletion experiments.

claim: Acute exercise induces changes in several known metabolic mediators of immune responses.
source: Acute exercise induces changes in several known metabolic mediators of immune responses (Henderson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Henderson et al., 2004.

claim: Exercise reduced the frequency of glycolytic metabolites in skeletal muscle, including fructose-6-phosphate, glucose-6-phosphate, and 3-phosphoglyceric acid.
source: Exercise affects a wide range of metabolic pathways; in particular, exercise reduced the frequency of glycolytic metabolites in skeletal muscle, for example, fructose-6-phosphate, glucose-6-phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3 PG), while the frequency of several of the TCA metabolites, for example, citric acid, fumaric acid and malic acid, were significantly higher in muscle post-exercise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise reduced glycolytic metabolites in muscle, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Exercise increased the frequency of TCA metabolites in skeletal muscle, including citric acid, fumaric acid, and malic acid.
source: Exercise affects a wide range of metabolic pathways; in particular, exercise reduced the frequency of glycolytic metabolites in skeletal muscle, for example, fructose-6-phosphate, glucose-6-phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3 PG), while the frequency of several of the TCA metabolites, for example, citric acid, fumaric acid and malic acid, were significantly higher in muscle post-exercise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise increased TCA metabolites in muscle, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mitochondrial metabolism is rate-limiting in high-intensity exertion.
source: This is in line with mitochondrial metabolism being rate-limiting in high-intensity exertion (Brooks, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brooks, 1998.

claim: TCA metabolites citric acid, malic acid, and alpha ketoglutaric acid were higher in plasma after exertion.
source: Interestingly, the TCA metabolites citric acid, malic acid and alpha ketoglutaric acid (aKG) were all higher in plasma after exertion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting release of these metabolites from muscle into plasma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that these TCA metabolites were higher in plasma after exercise, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Exercise causes release of TCA metabolites from muscle into plasma.
source: Interestingly, the TCA metabolites citric acid, malic acid and alpha ketoglutaric acid (aKG) were all higher in plasma after exertion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting release of these metabolites from muscle into plasma (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript suggests release of metabolites from muscle to plasma based on the observation of increased plasma levels, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: Contribution of muscle citrate to plasma has been shown by femoral arterio-venous sampling during exercise in human subjects.
source: Contribution of muscle citrate to plasma has previously been shown; for example, by femoral arterio-venous sampling during exercise in human subjects (Nielsen and Thomsen, 1979; Schranner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nielsen and Thomsen, 1979, and Schranner et al., 2020.

claim: Acute exercise altered the intramuscular and circulating levels of TCA metabolites in mice.
source: As well as altering the intramuscular (Figure 2B) and circulating levels of the TCA metabolites (Figure 2C and D), acute exercise in these experiments also introduced shifts in the metabolic profiles of lymphoid organs, supporting the notion that acute exercise alters the metabolic environment of lymphoid organs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise altered TCA metabolite levels, with data shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Acute exercise introduced shifts in the metabolic profiles of lymphoid organs in mice.
source: As well as altering the intramuscular (Figure 2B) and circulating levels of the TCA metabolites (Figure 2C and D), acute exercise in these experiments also introduced shifts in the metabolic profiles of lymphoid organs, supporting the notion that acute exercise alters the metabolic environment of lymphoid organs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that exercise altered metabolic profiles in lymphoid organs, with data shown in Figures 2E-G.

claim: The number of significantly increased metabolites was markedly higher in muscle draining lymph nodes compared to non-draining lymph nodes after exercise.
source: Notably, the number of significantly increased metabolites was markedly higher in the muscle draining lymph nodes when compared to non-draining lymph nodes (Figure 2F and G, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation, with data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Changes in metabolites seen in draining lymph nodes are likely attributable to muscle metabolite production.
source: This indicates that changes seen in draining lymph nodes are likely attributable to muscle metabolite production.

claim: Plasma, draining lymph nodes, and non-draining lymph nodes all showed higher levels of corticosterone after exercise.
source: Interestingly, plasma, draining lymph nodes, and non-draining lymph nodes all showed higher levels of corticosterone after exercise (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that corticosterone levels were higher in these tissues after exercise, with data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Changes in amino acid and fatty acid levels were identified in multiple organs after exercise.
source: Changes in amino acid and fatty acid levels were also identified in multiple organs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that changes in amino acid and fatty acid levels were identified, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The single most profound metabolic change induced by exertion is the transient increase in circulating lactate.
source: However, the single most profound metabolic change induced by exertion is the transient increase in circulating lactate.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the magnitude of lactate changes during exercise.

claim: Circulating lactate levels can increase up to 100-fold in skeletal muscle in response to high intensity exertion.
source: Circulating lactate levels rise very rapidly during exercise, and can (in response to high intensity exertion) increase up to 100-fold in skeletal muscle (Bonen et al., 1998; Spriet et al., 1987), with a concomitant increase of more than 10-fold in plasma (Goodwin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonen et al., 1998, and Spriet et al., 1987.

claim: Circulating lactate levels can increase more than 10-fold in plasma in response to high intensity exertion.
source: Circulating lactate levels rise very rapidly during exercise, and can (in response to high intensity exertion) increase up to 100-fold in skeletal muscle (Bonen et al., 1998; Spriet et al., 1987), with a concomitant increase of more than 10-fold in plasma (Goodwin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goodwin et al., 2007.

claim: Rapid postmortem accumulation of systemic lactate in response to global oxygen deprivation prevented differentiation of lactate levels in murine organ samples.
source: The rapid postmortem accumulation of systemic lactate in response to global oxygen deprivation made us unable to differentiate the lactate levels in murine organ samples (Donaldson and Lamont, 2013; Keltanen et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this technical limitation, with citations to Donaldson and Lamont, 2013, and Keltanen et al., 2015.

claim: An increase in lactate and TCA cycle metabolites was seen in human plasma post-exercise.
source: An increase in lactate as well as TCA cycle metabolites was however seen in human plasma post-exercise (Figure 2D) and when measuring lactate in blood from the tail vein in live animals directly after an acute treadmill exercise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that lactate and TCA metabolites increased in human plasma post-exercise, with data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Lactate and TCA metabolites returned to close to resting levels 1 hour after exercise in human samples.
source: In the human samples, these returned to close to resting levels 1 hr after exercise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in central carbon availability are likely conserved between mice and humans.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that metabolite levels returned to near baseline 1 hour post-exercise, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Changes in central carbon availability in response to exercise are likely conserved between mice and humans.
source: In the human samples, these returned to close to resting levels 1 hr after exercise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in central carbon availability are likely conserved between mice and humans.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation based on the similarity of metabolic changes observed in both mice and humans.

claim: Exercise can reduce tumor growth in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner.
source: As shown above, exercise can reduce tumor growth in a CD8+ T-cell-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement of the findings from the CD8+ depletion experiments.

claim: Metabolism and T-cell differentiation are tightly linked.
source: Given that metabolism and T-cell differentiation are tightly linked (O'Neill et al., 2016; Pearce, 2010), we next sought to determine whether any of the central carbon metabolites generated during exercise could be a determining factor in the action of CD8+ T cells in this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2016, and Pearce, 2010.

claim: None of the tested metabolites provided proliferative advantages to CD8+ T cells after 3 days of activation.
source: Although none of the metabolites provided proliferative advantages after 3 days of activation, malate, succinate, and aKG were notably well tolerated by the T-cells at high doses (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that no metabolites provided proliferative advantages, with data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Malate, succinate, and aKG were notably well tolerated by CD8+ T-cells at high doses.
source: Although none of the metabolites provided proliferative advantages after 3 days of activation, malate, succinate, and aKG were notably well tolerated by the T-cells at high doses (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: Activation of CD8+ T cells in the presence of increasing concentrations of pyruvate and citrate reduced CD8+ T cell expansion.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that pyruvate and citrate reduced T cell expansion, with data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: TCA metabolites can be transported across the plasma membrane with sodium carboxylate cotransporters.
source: TCA metabolites can be transported across the plasma membrane with sodium carboxylate cotransporters (Markovich, 2012).

source: For this reason, lactate produced during exercise does not significantly alter circulating plasma pH levels (unlike the acidification seen in, for example, solid tumors) (Brand et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brand et al., 2016.

source: Malate, succinate, fumarate, aKG, and lactate all induced a loss of CD62L at around 1 mM concentrations, (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Loss of CD62L surface expression is induced in response to TCR activation and is instrumental for the migratory capacity of cells localized in secondary lymphoid organs.
source: Loss of CD62L surface expression is induced in response to TCR activation and instrumental for the migratory capacity of cells localized in secondary lymphoid organs.

source: Furthermore, sodium L-lactate induced a dose-dependent increase in inducible T-cell costimulator (iCOS) and Granzyme B (GzmB) expression at day 3 of culture (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F).

claim: Sodium L-lactate induced a dose-dependent increase in Granzyme B (GzmB) expression at day 3 of culture in activated CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, sodium L-lactate induced a dose-dependent increase in inducible T-cell costimulator (iCOS) and Granzyme B (GzmB) expression at day 3 of culture (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that sodium L-lactate increased GzmB expression, with data shown in Figures 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: GzmB is the most highly expressed effector protein in activated mouse CD8+ T cells.
source: ICOS is expressed on activated T-cells and GzmB is the most highly expressed effector protein in activated mouse CD8+ T cells (Hukelmann et al., 2016) and is essential to granule-mediated apoptosis of target cells (Heusel et al., 1994).

source: To address if exercise can alter the central carbon metabolism of activated CD8+ T cells in vivo, we employed an OVA vaccination model and adoptive transfer of transgenic, OVA-specific OT-1 CD8+ T-cells where the timing of the T-cell activation can be controlled.

claim: Exercise altered the metabolism of activated CD8+ T cells in vivo at the level of m+3 labeled pyruvate and m+2 labeled aKG.

claim: Daily infusions of sodium L-lactate at 2 g/kg increased survival in C57BL/6 mice inoculated with MC38 colon adenocarcinoma cells.

claim: Previously proposed mechanisms for the anti-neoplastic effects of exercise include immune function.
source: Previously proposed underlying mechanisms for the anti-neoplastic effects of exercise include effects on weight control and endocrine hormone levels, as well as altered tumor vascularization (Betof et al., 2015) and immune function (Gleeson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gleeson et al., 2011.

claim: Exercise has been shown to reduce systemic inflammation.
source: Exercise has been shown to reduce systemic inflammation (Gleeson et al., 2011), cause increases in circulating numbers of immune cells (Gustafson et al., 2017) and enhance vaccination response (Ledo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gleeson et al., 2011.

claim: Exercise causes increases in circulating numbers of immune cells.
source: Exercise has been shown to reduce systemic inflammation (Gleeson et al., 2011), cause increases in circulating numbers of immune cells (Gustafson et al., 2017) and enhance vaccination response (Ledo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gustafson et al., 2017.

claim: Exercise enhances vaccination response.
source: Exercise has been shown to reduce systemic inflammation (Gleeson et al., 2011), cause increases in circulating numbers of immune cells (Gustafson et al., 2017) and enhance vaccination response (Ledo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ledo et al., 2020.

claim: Systemic levels of both CD8+ T cell and NK cell levels increase transiently in response to acute exercise.
source: Systemic levels of both CD8+ T cell and NK cell levels increase transiently in response to acute exercise.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the transient increase in immune cell populations during exercise.

claim: Immune cells that increase in response to acute exercise exhibit an effector phenotype.
source: There is evidence that these immune cells populations exhibit an effector phenotype (Campbell et al., 2009) and an increased peripheral tissue homing capacity (Krüger and Mooren, 2007), both important for anti-tumor activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2009.

claim: Immune cells that increase in response to acute exercise exhibit an increased peripheral tissue homing capacity.
source: There is evidence that these immune cells populations exhibit an effector phenotype (Campbell et al., 2009) and an increased peripheral tissue homing capacity (Krüger and Mooren, 2007), both important for anti-tumor activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krüger and Mooren, 2007.

claim: Systemic signaling from activated skeletal muscle to immune cell function has been attributed to skeletal muscle-derived myokines such as IL-6 and Oncostatin-M (OSM), and to catecholamine release.
source: Systemic signaling from activated skeletal muscle to immune cell function has been attributed previously to for example skeletal muscle-derived myokines such as IL-6 and Oncostatin-M (OSM), and to catecholamine release (Gleeson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gleeson et al., 2011.

claim: An increase in systemic levels of epinephrine during exercise together with skeletal muscle IL-6 can increase NK cell recruitment during tumorigenesis.
source: In a recent study, Hojman et al., showed that an increase in systemic levels of epinephrine during exercise together with skeletal muscle IL-6 could increase NK cell recruitment during tumorigenesis (Pedersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pedersen et al., 2016.

claim: In the mouse models employed in this study, limited infiltration and no effect of exercise on the CD3- NK1.1+ population was found.
source: However, in the mouse models employed here we found limited infiltration and no effect of exercise on the CD3- NK1.1+ population, relative to our observation of an increased frequency of CD3+/CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the lack of NK cell effects in the authors' models.

claim: The results from depletion and adoptive transfer of the CD8+ population provide support for the importance of cytotoxic T-cells in mediating the anti-neoplastic effects of exercise.
source: The results from depletion and adoptive transfer of the CD8+ population provide further support for the importance of cytotoxic T-cells in mediating the anti-neoplastic effects of exercise.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Different metabolic environments can instruct effector functions of immune cells.
source: Immune cells patrol all corners of the body and can reside in niches with highly differential metabolic profiles. Recent findings have provided evidence that these different environments can instruct effector functions of immune cells (Buck et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buck et al., 2017.

claim: Exercise modulates metabolic parameters significantly beyond local skeletal muscle.
source: In the current study, we show how exercise modulates metabolic parameters significantly beyond local skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is an explicit summary of the metabolomic findings.

claim: Lactate and TCA metabolites accumulated in both the active skeletal muscle and in plasma and secondary lymphoid organs after acute exertion.
source: We found that lactate and TCA metabolites accumulated in both the active skeletal muscle and in plasma and secondary lymphoid organs after acute exertion.
evidence: This is an explicit summary of the metabolomic findings.

claim: The principal shaping of immune function happens at the point of activation, primarily occurring in the lymphoid organs.
source: As trafficking immune cells circulate, they will often be exposed to high levels of accumulating metabolites, in both loci of disease and in metabolically active tissues. However, the principal shaping of immune function happens at the point of activation, primarily occurring in the lymphoid organs.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about where immune cell activation primarily occurs.

claim: Key metabolites, including lactate, had unexpected functions in the activation of CD8+ T cells.
source: In evaluating the role an altered metabolic environment plays in the process of modifying CD8+ T-cell function, we found that key metabolites, including lactate, had unexpected functions in the activation of CD8+ T cells, with multiple TCA metabolites stimulating the loss of CD62L.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the unexpected findings regarding metabolite effects on T cells.

claim: CD62L shedding from TCR activated CD8+ T-cells has been suggested to be mTOR and PI3K dependent.
source: CD62L shedding from TCR activated CD8+ T-cells has been suggested to be mTOR and PI3K dependent (Sinclair et al., 2008) and aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in multiple cell lines (DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Durán et al., 2013; Villar et al., 2015), as well as in activated CD8+ T-cells (Suzuki et al., 2018), suggesting that the metabolite-induced loss of CD62L may be mediated through mTOR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sinclair et al., 2008.

claim: aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in multiple cell lines.
source: CD62L shedding from TCR activated CD8+ T-cells has been suggested to be mTOR and PI3K dependent (Sinclair et al., 2008) and aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in multiple cell lines (DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Durán et al., 2013; Villar et al., 2015), as well as in activated CD8+ T-cells (Suzuki et al., 2018), suggesting that the metabolite-induced loss of CD62L may be mediated through mTOR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Durán et al., 2013; and Villar et al., 2015.

claim: aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in activated CD8+ T-cells.
source: CD62L shedding from TCR activated CD8+ T-cells has been suggested to be mTOR and PI3K dependent (Sinclair et al., 2008) and aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in multiple cell lines (DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Durán et al., 2013; Villar et al., 2015), as well as in activated CD8+ T-cells (Suzuki et al., 2018), suggesting that the metabolite-induced loss of CD62L may be mediated through mTOR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2018.

claim: The metabolite-induced loss of CD62L may be mediated through mTOR activation.
source: CD62L shedding from TCR activated CD8+ T-cells has been suggested to be mTOR and PI3K dependent (Sinclair et al., 2008) and aKG-mediated activation of mTORC1 has been reported in multiple cell lines (DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Durán et al., 2013; Villar et al., 2015), as well as in activated CD8+ T-cells (Suzuki et al., 2018), suggesting that the metabolite-induced loss of CD62L may be mediated through mTOR activation.
evidence: This is an explicit speculation based on the cited literature and the authors' findings.

claim: Within the local micro-environment, tumor-derived lactate has been shown to inhibit the antitumor functions of both T and NK cells due to intracellular acidification.
source: In contrast to our findings, within the local micro-environment, tumor-derived lactate has been shown to inhibit the antitumor functions of both T and NK cells due to intracellular acidification (Brand et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brand et al., 2016.

claim: Lactate-associated acidity has been shown to impair CD8+ T cell motility.
source: Likewise, lactate-associated acidity has been shown to impair CD8+ T cell motility (Haas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haas et al., 2015.

claim: Within poorly vascularized and fast-growing tumor masses, or in laboratory ex vivo cultures, lactic acid export from cells results in a significant acidosis.
source: Importantly, within poorly vascularized and fast-growing tumor masses, or in laboratory ex vivo cultures, lactic acid export from cells results in a significant acidosis.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the conditions under which lactate causes acidosis.

claim: Healthy tissue microenvironments are very efficiently buffered and capable of maintaining a physiological pH range even when large amounts of lactate are produced.
source: However, healthy tissue microenvironments are very efficiently buffered, and capable of maintaining a physiological pH range even when large amounts of lactate are produced.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the buffering capacity of healthy tissues.

claim: Circulating levels of TCA metabolites increase by 2-8 fold after exercise.
source: Our findings that circulating levels of TCA metabolites increase by 2–8 fold after exercise suggests that at peripheral sites, substantial amounts of these metabolites have been released into the lymphatic fluid draining the muscle tissue.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the magnitude of TCA metabolite increases.

claim: At peripheral sites, substantial amounts of TCA metabolites have been released into the lymphatic fluid draining the muscle tissue after exercise.
source: Our findings that circulating levels of TCA metabolites increase by 2–8 fold after exercise suggests that at peripheral sites, substantial amounts of these metabolites have been released into the lymphatic fluid draining the muscle tissue.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation of the metabolite data.

claim: TCA metabolites are readily available in mesenteric lymph.
source: Additionally, a recent paper using lymphatic cannulation showed that TCA metabolites are readily available in, for example, mesenteric lymph (Zawieja et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zawieja et al., 2019.

claim: The use of distally produced lactate as a fuel for oxidative respiration was described for inactive muscle in 1970.
source: The use of distally produced lactate as a fuel for oxidative respiration was described for inactive muscle already in 1970 (Jorfeldt, 1970) and has recently been reported in both malignant and non-malignant cell types (Faubert et al., 2017; Hui et al., 2017), suggesting that lactate can be used as a primary fuel by CD8+ T cells, at least during early activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jorfeldt, 1970.

claim: Lactate can be used as a fuel for oxidative respiration in both malignant and non-malignant cell types.
source: The use of distally produced lactate as a fuel for oxidative respiration was described for inactive muscle already in 1970 (Jorfeldt, 1970) and has recently been reported in both malignant and non-malignant cell types (Faubert et al., 2017; Hui et al., 2017), suggesting that lactate can be used as a primary fuel by CD8+ T cells, at least during early activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Faubert et al., 2017, and Hui et al., 2017.

claim: Lactate can be used as a primary fuel by CD8+ T cells, at least during early activation.
source: The use of distally produced lactate as a fuel for oxidative respiration was described for inactive muscle already in 1970 (Jorfeldt, 1970) and has recently been reported in both malignant and non-malignant cell types (Faubert et al., 2017; Hui et al., 2017), suggesting that lactate can be used as a primary fuel by CD8+ T cells, at least during early activation.
evidence: This is an explicit speculation based on the cited literature.

claim: Dilution of 13C labeling between glycolysis and TCA cycle intermediates can imply oxidation of alternative fuels.
source: Dilution of 13C labeling between glycolysis and TCA cycle intermediates can imply oxidation of alternative fuels (Hensley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al., 2016.

claim: The administered 13C-glucose was used as a carbon source by CD8+ T cells.
source: The administered 13C-glucose was, as expected, used as a carbon source by CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the use of labeled glucose by T cells.

claim: Total glucose levels were similar between T-cells from exercising and non-exercising animals.
source: Although total glucose levels were similar between T-cells from exercising and non-exercising animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the availability of labeled glucose appeared lower in exercised animals, reflected by lower total 13C-glucose counts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that total glucose levels were similar, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The availability of labeled glucose appeared lower in exercised animals, reflected by lower total 13C-glucose counts.
source: Although total glucose levels were similar between T-cells from exercising and non-exercising animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the availability of labeled glucose appeared lower in exercised animals, reflected by lower total 13C-glucose counts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that labeled glucose availability was lower in exercised animals, with data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduced availability of labeled glucose in exercised animals is most likely due to dilution of the 13C-glucose in the circulating blood glucose pool due to a contribution from hepatic glycogenolysis, stimulated by the increased metabolic demand during exercise.
source: The reduced availability is most likely due to dilution of the 13C-glucose in the circulating blood glucose pool due to a contribution from hepatic glycogenolysis, stimulated by the increased metabolic demand during exercise.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation of the reduced labeled glucose availability.

claim: When normalized to the labeled glucose fraction, exercise altered the central carbon metabolism of activated CD8+ T-cells in vivo at the level of m+3 labeled pyruvate and m+2 labeled aKG.
source: When normalized to the labeled glucose fraction, exercise altered the central carbon metabolism of activated CD8+T-cells in vivo at the level of m+3 labeled pyruvate and m+2 labeled aKG.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the normalized metabolite data.

claim: The finding of altered m+3 pyruvate and m+2 aKG suggests an increased uptake of systemic metabolites by activated T-cells during exercise.
source: This finding suggests an increased uptake of systemic metabolites by activated T-cells during exercise.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation of the isotope labeling data.

claim: In the experimental setting where animals were given daily doses of high levels of sodium L-lactate, an increase in intratumoral CD8+ T-cells was found.
source: In the experimental setting where animals were given daily doses of high levels of sodium L-lactate, we found an increase in intratumoral CD8+ T-cells and a decrease in overall tumor growth.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the findings from the lactate administration experiments.

claim: In the experimental setting where animals were given daily doses of high levels of sodium L-lactate, a decrease in overall tumor growth was found.
source: In the experimental setting where animals were given daily doses of high levels of sodium L-lactate, we found an increase in intratumoral CD8+ T-cells and a decrease in overall tumor growth.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the findings from the lactate administration experiments.

claim: High levels of CD4+ cells were found in tumors after daily lactate administration.
source: In addition, we found high levels of CD4+ cells and reduced NK-cell infiltration, supporting previous evidence that lactate can affect multiple cells of the immune system.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the findings from the lactate administration experiments.

claim: Reduced NK-cell infiltration was found in tumors after daily lactate administration.
source: In addition, we found high levels of CD4+ cells and reduced NK-cell infiltration, supporting previous evidence that lactate can affect multiple cells of the immune system.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the findings from the lactate administration experiments.

claim: Lactate can affect multiple cells of the immune system.
source: In addition, we found high levels of CD4+ cells and reduced NK-cell infiltration, supporting previous evidence that lactate can affect multiple cells of the immune system.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation supported by the observed effects on multiple immune cell types.

claim: Lactate infusion mimics some of the effects of exercise, but exercise has additional, integrative components beyond merely increased levels of lactate.
source: These findings indicate that lactate infusion mimics some of the effects of exercise, but that exercise has additional, integrative, components beyond merely increased levels of lactate.
evidence: This is an explicit interpretation comparing the effects of lactate infusion to exercise.

claim: The antitumoral effects of exercise depend on CD8+ T-cells.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that the antitumoral effects of exercise depend on CD8+ T-cells, and that intense exertion can alter the intrinsic metabolism and antitumoral effector function of cytotoxic T-cells.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Intense exertion can alter the intrinsic metabolism and antitumoral effector function of cytotoxic T-cells.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that the antitumoral effects of exercise depend on CD8+ T-cells, and that intense exertion can alter the intrinsic metabolism and antitumoral effector function of cytotoxic T-cells.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement of the main findings.

claim: In the physiological setting, exercise-derived metabolites, whether systemically delivered or draining into an adjacent lymph node, could act to boost a nascent T cell response.
source: This indicates that, in the physiological setting, exercise-derived metabolites, whether systemically delivered or draining into an adjacent lymph node, could act to boost a nascent T cell response.
evidence: This is an explicit speculation about the physiological role of exercise-derived metabolites.

claim: The adaptive immune system is a key component of exercise-induced suppression of tumorigenesis.
source: This indicates that the adaptive immune system is a key component of exercise-induced suppression of tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is an explicit conclusion drawn from the overall findings.

claim: FVB inbred mice are enthusiastic runners relative to most other inbred strains.
source: FVB inbred mice are enthusiastic runners relative to most other inbred strains (Avila et al., 2017), and the MMTV-PyMT model in many regard mimics the gradual progression of human breast cancer (Lin et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Avila et al., 2017.

claim: The MMTV-PyMT model in many regards mimics the gradual progression of human breast cancer.
source: FVB inbred mice are enthusiastic runners relative to most other inbred strains (Avila et al., 2017), and the MMTV-PyMT model in many regard mimics the gradual progression of human breast cancer (Lin et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2003.

claim: PyMT+ mice ran on average 6 km/day.
source: PyMT+ mice ran on average 6 km/day (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the average running distance, with data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An intraperitoneal injection of a 2 g/kg dose of sodium L-lactate results in an 18 mM spike in serum lactate concentrations at 20 min post-injection.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, an intraperitoneal injection of a 2 g/kg dose of sodium L-lactate results in a 18 mM spike in serum lactate concentrations at 20 min post-injection.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the magnitude and timing of the lactate spike, with data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Following a 2 g/kg dose of sodium L-lactate, serum lactate levels subside to 4 mM within 60 min.
source: Following this dose, levels subside to 4 mM within 60 min; the expected time to reach baseline values from this magnitude of spike is approximately 180 min post-injection (Lezi et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lactate levels at 60 min.

claim: The expected time to reach baseline lactate values from an 18 mM spike is approximately 180 min post-injection.
source: Following this dose, levels subside to 4 mM within 60 min; the expected time to reach baseline values from this magnitude of spike is approximately 180 min post-injection (Lezi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lezi et al., 2013.

claim: In humans, exercising cohorts have lower rates of cancer incidence.
source: In humans, exercising cohorts have lower rates of cancer incidence (Moore et al., 2016) and better outcomes across a range of cancer diagnoses (Cormie et al., 2017; Friedenreich et al., 2016), proportionate to the degree and intensity of exercise.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2016.

claim: In humans, exercising cohorts have better outcomes across a range of cancer diagnoses.
source: In humans, exercising cohorts have lower rates of cancer incidence (Moore et al., 2016) and better outcomes across a range of cancer diagnoses (Cormie et al., 2017; Friedenreich et al., 2016), proportionate to the degree and intensity of exercise.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cormie et al., 2017, and Friedenreich et al., 2016.

claim: The beneficial effects of exercise on cancer outcomes are proportionate to the degree and intensity of exercise.
source: In humans, exercising cohorts have lower rates of cancer incidence (Moore et al., 2016) and better outcomes across a range of cancer diagnoses (Cormie et al., 2017; Friedenreich et al., 2016), proportionate to the degree and intensity of exercise.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the dose-response relationship between exercise and cancer outcomes.

claim: Recent work has indicated a relationship between immune response and exercise-induced changes in malignant progression.
source: The mechanisms underlying these observations have remained elusive, although recent work has indicated a relationship between immune response and exercise-induced changes in malignant progression (Pedersen et al., 2016; Koelwyn et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pedersen et al., 2016, and Koelwyn et al., 2017.

claim: The metabolic demands of strenuous physical exertion generally induce significant changes in nutrient utilization, principally via central carbon metabolism.
source: The metabolic demands of strenuous physical exertion generally induce significant changes in nutrient utilization, principally via central carbon metabolism (Brooks, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brooks, 1998.

claim: Exercise-induced alterations in metabolism change the ratios of energy substrates utilized and can shift intramuscular metabolite profiles.
source: These exercise-induced alterations in metabolism change the ratios of energy substrates utilized, and can shift intramuscular metabolite profiles.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the metabolic effects of exercise.

claim: Shifts in intramuscular metabolite profiles are reflected in systemic metabolite availability, which in turn modifies energy production throughout the body.
source: These shifts are reflected in systemic metabolite availability, which in turn modifies energy production throughout the body (Henderson et al., 2004; Lezi et al., 2013; El Hayek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henderson et al., 2004; Lezi et al., 2013; and El Hayek et al., 2019.

claim: Cytotoxic T cells play a crucial role in controlling tumor growth.
source: It is clear that cytotoxic T cells play a crucial role in controlling tumor growth.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the role of cytotoxic T cells in tumor control.

claim: T cells can identify and eliminate malignant cells by recognizing mutation-derived neoantigens in a process known as immunosurveillance.
source: By recognizing mutation-derived neoantigens, T cells can identify and eliminate malignant cells in a process known as immunosurveillance (Dunn et al., 2002; Dunn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2002, and Dunn et al., 2004.

claim: Escape from immune control is a critical step toward progressive malignant growth in many cancers.
source: Escape from immune control is a critical step toward progressive malignant growth in many cancers, and tumors achieve this in a number of ways, amongst them the dampening of antitumor T cell responses (Dunn et al., 2002; Dunn et al., 2004; Beatty and Gladney, 2015; Zappasodi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2002; Dunn et al., 2004; Beatty and Gladney, 2015; and Zappasodi et al., 2018.

claim: Tumors achieve immune escape through dampening of antitumor T cell responses.
source: Escape from immune control is a critical step toward progressive malignant growth in many cancers, and tumors achieve this in a number of ways, amongst them the dampening of antitumor T cell responses (Dunn et al., 2002; Dunn et al., 2004; Beatty and Gladney, 2015; Zappasodi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2002; Dunn et al., 2004; Beatty and Gladney, 2015; and Zappasodi et al., 2018.

claim: The activity of immune cells is tightly linked with their metabolism.
source: The activity of immune cells is tightly linked with their metabolism (O'Neill et al., 2016; Pearce and Pearce, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Neill et al., 2016, and Pearce and Pearce, 2013.

claim: Many aspects of immune cell energetics are likely sensitive to the metabolic changes induced by exercise.
source: Many aspects of immune cell energetics are likely sensitive to the metabolic changes induced by exercise (Henderson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Henderson et al., 2004.

claim: Exercise is known to affect immune cell function.
source: Exercise is known to affect immune cell function, and an altered immune response has been suggested as a mechanism underlying effects of exercise on cancer risk and progression (Christensen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the known effects of exercise on immune cells.

claim: An altered immune response has been suggested as a mechanism underlying effects of exercise on cancer risk and progression.
source: Exercise is known to affect immune cell function, and an altered immune response has been suggested as a mechanism underlying effects of exercise on cancer risk and progression (Christensen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Christensen et al., 2018.

claim: Exercise itself can modify cytotoxic T-cell metabolism.
source: We found that exercise itself can modify cytotoxic T-cell metabolism, and that exercise-induced effects on tumor growth are dependent on cytotoxic T-cell activity.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Exercise-induced effects on tumor growth are dependent on cytotoxic T-cell activity.
source: We found that exercise itself can modify cytotoxic T-cell metabolism, and that exercise-induced effects on tumor growth are dependent on cytotoxic T-cell activity.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Metabolites produced in skeletal muscle and excreted into plasma at high levels during exertion in both mice and humans enhance the effector profile of CD8+ T-cells.
source: We show here that in mice, exercise-induced reduction in tumor growth is dependent on CD8+ T cells, and that metabolites produced in skeletal muscle and excreted into plasma at high levels during exertion in both mice and humans enhance the effector profile of CD8+ T-cells.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement from the abstract.

claim: Activated murine CD8+ T cells alter their central carbon metabolism in response to exertion in vivo.
source: We found that activated murine CD8+ T cells alter their central carbon metabolism in response to exertion in vivo, and that immune cells from trained mice are more potent antitumor effector cells when transferred into tumor-bearing untrained animals.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement from the abstract.

claim: Immune cells from trained mice are more potent antitumor effector cells when transferred into tumor-bearing untrained animals.
source: We found that activated murine CD8+ T cells alter their central carbon metabolism in response to exertion in vivo, and that immune cells from trained mice are more potent antitumor effector cells when transferred into tumor-bearing untrained animals.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement from the abstract.

claim: CD8+ T cells are metabolically altered by exercise in a manner that acts to improve their antitumoral efficacy.
source: These data demonstrate that CD8+ T cells are metabolically altered by exercise in a manner that acts to improve their antitumoral efficacy.
evidence: This is an explicit summary statement from the abstract.
